This change also gives us the opportunity to allow disabling the 2D main screen in addition to the others (currently in 3.2 and master it is force-enabled), since now the logic is no longer dependent on either the 2D or 3D main screens being enabled. The 2D viewport is not necessary in a variety of situations (ex: making command line apps in Godot, making 3D game prototypes without a GUI, making 2.5D games with the [2.5D main screen plugin](https://godotengine.org/asset-library/asset/583), etc). This can be done in a follow-up PR (EDIT: #41038).

For this PR in particular, defaulting to 3D (as in current 3.2 and master) is rather arbitrary, so I guess it makes sense to default to whatever the first item in the list is unless someone has a reason against this. Even if we want to keep 3D as the default, the logic should still be changed to be similar to this PR, so that there are more fallbacks available.

body:
We don't need to perform the dot product twice, the values on each side are inversely related, matching up at `Math_SQRT12`. So we can just compare with `Math_SQRT12`.

```suggestion
		should_switch = abs(Vector2(1, 0).rotated(angle).dot(Vector2(1, 0))) < Math_SQRT12;
```

By the way, this is similar to what I initially suggested above, but using `Vector2(1, 0).rotated(angle)` instead of `x.normalized()` for the rotation.

body: That is a very specific name for a general feature. `calt` might not be used for ligatures (an Arabic or Indic monospaced font for instance), and ”coding ligatures” might use other features like `liga`. Either make the name reflect what the code is actually doing (not the its intent) or make it a general OpenType features control.
author: khaledhosny

body:
> or make it a general OpenType features control.

The Editor Settings dialog can only expose simple booleans, integers, floats, colors, or "fixed" enums, not an enum that's dynamically constructed based on the currently loaded font.

Most casual users will search for "ligatures", so that word should definitely be present in the setting name. (Search bases itself on the setting's name only, since we don't have a description for each setting yet.)
author: Calinou

body: A fixed `enum` should work, the [number of OpenType features](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/typography/opentype/spec/featurelist) is finite, and though the list is long, many of the features are required (for proper text layout) and should not be controllable.
author: khaledhosny

body:
Fixed enum won't give full control, since some features can be set to the integer value not just enabled/disabled (swashes and other stylistic features), and each feature can be applied to the sub range of the string.

For generic controls, OT features are currently set as the single string property (e.g `swsh=2,lnum,zero`), but for the code editor it's probably better to have some fixed list too, maybe:

- `code_font_ligatures` → (enum) "Default, Disable ligatures, Use custom OT features"
- `code_font_ot_features` → (string) for full control, used if "custom" is selected.
author: bruvzg

body:
> `code_font_ligatures` → (enum) "Default, Disable ligatures, Use custom OT features"

My point is that a name like `code_font_ligatures` is misleading, if you really want to control `calt` (though I’m pretty sure there are ”coding fonts” using `liga`), just call it what it is; contextual ligatures.
author: khaledhosny

body: At least "Fira Code", "Iosevka" and "JetBrains Mono" use `calt` to control coding ligatures `liga` do not affect it at all.

body: What is the downside about having large branches?
author: clayjohn

body:
> What is the downside about having large branches?

It is a complicated relationship from what I could see. On a very basic level, having larger branches is quicker for editing (moving objects around, inserting, erasing), but can be slower in certain types of test (particularly those in physics).

However, the difference due to editing is a one off cost within a frame (or tick), whereas the cost for testing depends how many tests are done.

For instance for visibility, it most situations I have tested there is benefit from having larger branches. It could be argued to have the default set higher, however at the moment I am tending towards a setting which can give a performance increase when tweaked, rather than one that can remove a performance drop when tweaked.

For visibility, in a lot of cases there may only be one or a few tests performed on the octree, hence the balance for editing speed is usually better. However, if you were making a game that made a large number of visibility tests the balance could shift the other way.

For godot physics on the other hand, with a large number of objects (thousands) and thus many thousands of tests, smaller branches always seemed to be better. Hence removing the new tree from there unless evidence shows it can lead to better performance.

Indeed, that's the problem. I've already mentioned it in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/41239#issuecomment-1335792985) (and suggested another possible solution). If going for separating the API (again, can't tell if that's the preffered way of solving it) then I think it'd make more sense to keep the same prefix in both methods for easier discoverability, e.g. something like `draw_line`+`draw_line_primitive` / `draw_line_quad`+`draw_line` / `draw_line_quad`+`draw_line_primitive` / etc.

>For the "thin rectangle" variant (which doesn't change line thickness when scaled), we have to consider the CanvasItem's transform?

If we'd want to keep auto-detecting when to use line primitive over the quad and make it be done only when the actual result is thin (instead of when the rect is locally thin like it's currently done) then yeah, all the transforms which will affect the final CanvasItem render would need to be taken into account. But I don't think it's easily feasible as the decision which primitive to use (line/quad) would need to be probably postponed to when the RenderingServer actually issues stuff to be rendered. And actually I think auto detection might be not wanted as it might be break batching. It seems that primitives with different point count (like lines and quads) are currently not batched together. Which means using always quads could be potentially more performant than sometimes using line primitives. So yeah, I still think just giving the choice for quad/line to the user is the way to go.

Errors can often get repeated but not contiguous, e.g.:
```
ERROR: get_action_strength: Request for nonexistent InputMap action 'look_right'.
   At: main/input_default.cpp:142.
ERROR: get_action_strength: Request for nonexistent InputMap action 'look_left'.
   At: main/input_default.cpp:142.
ERROR: get_action_strength: Request for nonexistent InputMap action 'look_down'.
   At: main/input_default.cpp:142.
ERROR: get_action_strength: Request for nonexistent InputMap action 'look_up'.
   At: main/input_default.cpp:142.
ERROR: get_action_strength: Request for nonexistent InputMap action 'look_right'.
   At: main/input_default.cpp:142.
ERROR: get_action_strength: Request for nonexistent InputMap action 'look_left'.
   At: main/input_default.cpp:142.
ERROR: get_action_strength: Request for nonexistent InputMap action 'look_down'.
   At: main/input_default.cpp:142.
ERROR: get_action_strength: Request for nonexistent InputMap action 'look_up'.
   At: main/input_default.cpp:142.
ERROR: get_action_strength: Request for nonexistent InputMap action 'look_right'.
   At: main/input_default.cpp:142.
ERROR: get_action_strength: Request for nonexistent InputMap action 'look_left'.
   At: main/input_default.cpp:142.
ERROR: get_action_strength: Request for nonexistent InputMap action 'look_down'.
   At: main/input_default.cpp:142.
ERROR: get_action_strength: Request for nonexistent InputMap action 'look_up'.
   At: main/input_default.cpp:142.
```

Typically happens when triggering multiple errors in a given frame which are then repeated each frame. It can also happen with chained errors when the engine prints several error messages for a single fault (e.g. when a scene can't be loaded due to missing imported dependencies).

Is this something we could handle? That would require storing all messages in a hashmap to increment the counter regardless of the position, that might impact performance I guess.

Alternatively this could maybe be done over e.g. the last 10 messages, so it would group related duplicate messages which happen in close sequence, but not a later similar message spam from another source. (E.g. physics errors triggered by two different physics body that the player interacts with at different times.)

body:
I don't think this change is a good idea. While I appreciate the desire for physically accurate physics, physically accurate physics is not intuitive to users. (e.g. when damping is physically accurate: #19182). Similarly, I expect this change to confuse users.

Intuitively, gravity at or near the `Gravity Point` is not expected to be infinite, it's expected to be equal to `Gravity`. With any `Gravity Distance Scale` > 0, gravity at the `Gravity Point` is still expected to be equal to `Gravity`; and then drop off with distance at a rate proportional to the `Gravity Distance Scale`. However, with this change, gravity near the `Gravity Point` would now be nearly infinite (regardless of whether or not a warning is raised).

Most importantly, with this change, there is no way to achieve the current behaviour. It would either by equal to `Gravity` and not vary with distance, or it would be infinite at the `Gravity Point` and only finally equal `Gravity` at a distance equal to the `Gravity Scale` before dropping off as it did before.

If physically accurate gravity is required, the user can always override physics with the `Custom Integrator`; including taking responsibility for ensuring the attractor has a volume. The lack of a volume being the real reason the gravity around a `Gravity Point` cannot be physically accurate.

Finally, even if this change is still desired, it should be updated to include Bullet physics too.

body: Why `2.0 * Math_PI` to wrap to `(-pi, pi)`? Also, prefer `Math_TAU` to `2.0 * Math_PI`.
author: aaronfranke

body:
The remainder function takes the (signed) distance between the first parameter and the nearest integer multiple of the second value. By way of analogy, remainder is to rounding as the modulus is to truncation.

It may help to mentally step through all of the ranges for the angle. Between 0 and pi, the nearest integer multiple of 2\*pi is 0, so the angle is unchanged. Between pi and 2\*pi, the nearest integer multiple is 2pi, and the distance is `angle - 2*pi` (negative, because the angle is less than the nearest multiple), so the angle gets transformed to the range (-pi, 0), which is correct. Similarly, between -pi to 0, the nearest multiple is 0 and the angle is unchanged. Between -2pi and -pi, the nearest angle is -2pi and the distance is `angle - (-2pi)`.
author: keegano
aaronfranke

body:
I agree that the remainder function is confusingly-named. However, I think we don't need to make a habit of describing functions from the standard library wherever they are used.

Perhaps it would be better to define an inline wrap_angle function to make it clearer the intent of this line, and that way the implementation could also be changed with something more performant later if someone decided to do that. 

I also prefer 2.0*Math_PI in this case, because it makes the relationship to the range (-pi, pi) more explicit. 

That said as of right now this is the only place I'm aware of where angle wrapping is needed, so I'd lean against adding complexity and optimization prematurely. This is a bugfix PR, another PR could be used to redesign (and if I were doing that, I'd change to a stable angle-between-vectors algorithm instead of subtracting angles).
author: keegano

body: We do have `fposmod`, which works for angles, but gives outputs on the range (0, TAU) if used with TAU or 2PI, so we would have to add a check with `> Math_PI` and then do `-= Math_TAU`.

body:
> Discuss: Depending on how get_csv_line should behave, [""] could also be a valid return, but it makes it difficult to tell when EOF has been reached.

With the current state of this PR, it is still difficult to tell when EOF has been reached. The length for an empty line in the middle of the file is the same as for at the end of the file. So I'm not sure how this change helps this particular goal.

```gdscript
func _save():
	var file := File.new()
	file.open(path, File.WRITE)
	file.store_csv_line(["a", "b", "c"])
	file.store_csv_line([])
	file.store_csv_line(["d", "e", "f"])
	file.close()

func _load():
	var file := File.new()
	file.open(path, File.READ)
	print(file.get_csv_line().size()) # 3
	print(file.get_csv_line().size()) # 0
	print(file.get_csv_line().size()) # 3
	print(file.get_csv_line().size()) # 0
	file.close()
```

That said, the change itself seems good, indeed there are 0 items on these lines, so this change makes sense to me. I don't think that `[""]` would be better. Therefore I'm giving this an approval.

body:
I don't think it can be done inside the switch case - we have to consume the IN before parsing the right operand and that means checking for, and special-casing, `op == NOT` in every call to `parse_binary_operator`. Not a huge hit, performance-wise, but still easily avoidable by just adding this new function and switching to it in the prefix/infix table that will be checked anyway. It's the only operator that consists of two tokens, the new function seems to be a clean way to hide that from `parse_binary_operator`.

Changing `previous` was necessary since that indicates the type of operator inside `parse_binary_operator` and it's only one token, so NOT had to get there to differentiate it from a plain IN. But with the previous comment re: expanding NOT IN into to two operations instead of a new Variant operator, manipulating `previous` won't be necessary any more, so I'll change that.

However, I still think the new function is better than having an `if` in every call to `parse_binary_operator`. What do you think @vnen ?

body:
I don't think the right language is used here. The call doesn't actually "propagate" from what I can tell (see `SceneTree::_call_input_pause`). 

> The input event propagates up through the node tree

This language might mislead the user into thinking the call is repeated on parents until it is handled, or until the last parent. This is not correct. `call_input_pause` only calls the method on the node it is registered to call on. For example, MenuButtons are registered to receive `unhandled_key_input`. The `_unhandled_key_input` method is only called on the MenuButton - not parents, and not children.

I would probably change this to something more accurate:
"`_unhandled_input` is called on every node which is registered to receive it until one of the nodes handles the input."

However this relies on the information that "It is only called if unhandled input processing is enabled" so this might be better to place after the next line
The usage of the word "propagates" may also mislead the user into thinking at `Object::propagate_call` is used behind the scenes for this functionality. 

It may also be worth noting that the order of the nodes it is called on is based on order in the scene tree - based on `Node::is_greater_than`.
author: EricEzaM

body: P.S. I know this isn't part of the PR but I thought since we are here, let's discuss
author: EricEzaM

body: My comment above also applies here.
author: EricEzaM

body:
You are right on all the points, but to be honest I don't think we should care that much.
The function is indeed not called on all the nodes, as they indeed have to implement the method. I am not sure it is worth mentioning to the user, as they probably know know an unexisting function cannot be called.

Regarding the "propagate" term, in the end it's the same. It's a similar behavior to calling `Node::propagate_call`, as the node order produced by `Node::is_greater_than` will lead to the same order as what a reversed propagate_call would do. That's why the documentation mentions "propagates up through the node tree".

We have to write the documentation from the user point of view, what happen behind the scene for performance reasons (like adding the nodes to a group, so that the function is only called on specific nodes, etc...) is not important. What matters is the end result.

There are two ways to fix this:
1. Modify the behavior so that `insert_before(null, value)` pushes to the front of the list instead of back.
2. Actually handle this case as an error (for both `insert_before(null, value)` and `insert_after(null, value)`), because you can always check whether an element is valid beforehand and decide whether you want to insert a new value elsewhere.

body:
The physics engines do clamp the calculated bounce to 0..1:
```
body_pair_2d_sw.cpp
214:real_t combine_bounce(Body2DSW *A, Body2DSW *B) {
215:    return CLAMP(A->get_bounce() + B->get_bounce(), 0, 1);
```
(at least in 2D)

Sure you can set a negative bounce on one body of -5.0 and the other one +5.5 and they should amount to +0.5 and be within bounds... But why? We don't cater to undefined use cases, and if there's no implemented physics engine that actually *supports* values outside 0..1 (as in, it's designed in a way where those values actually make sense, not that they can incidentally produce an outcome which is not outright a bug), there's no reason to future proof.

If you have a very non-standard use case, you can use a script to set those values to arbitrary values. Or create a UnlimitedPhysicsMaterial resource in a script :)

We can discuss this in https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals, but I don't see the point in allowing values that don't make sense currently in the engine.

Input buffering and agile flushing are different concepts:
- Whether input buffering is used or not is up to each platform. (In the last refactor I accidentally removed this line from `OS_Android`: `input->set_use_input_buffering(true);`.)
- Agile input flushing is user opt-in. It will only work if the platform does input buffering. Otherwise, the events will be flushed once per idle frame (the classic behavior), as if agile flushing was disabled.

body: I've seen this warning multiple times from many sources, but still don't understand the why's of it. I also continue to not understand how to know when an texture is "imported" properly v.s. just present. There is also an implication that "imported" objects are inside the project folder before the game is exported but I've not seen this clearly defined. Lastly what should someone do if they truly intend for an image/texture to be loaded from `user://`?
author: xarses

body:
In theory this should be documented at [`Import process`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/getting_started/workflow/assets/import_process.html) page describing the reasons why assets like images have to be imported in Godot.

By default, any foreign file format is not recognized by Godot, so it will be ignored and not visible throughout the "FileSystem" dock (which looks into `res://` path, which happens to be a project's root on your filesystem, or the contents of `game.pck` when you export a project).

On the high-level, files like `*.png` are recognized by Godot, but they have to be made compatible with the existing datatypes first, like `Image` or `Texture`. Therefore, those foreign files have to be converted first, aka imported as `Resource`s. Those imported resources get saved into the `.import` folder which is hidden in Godot's UI.

The problem is that there may be different ways to convert such files, so the "Import" dock gives you the ability to configure the default import procedure for each file, as described in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/20972#issuecomment-645514487.

Now, if you want to actually interact with those imported resources, loading them by the "original path" is enough:

```gdscript
var texture = load("res://icon.png")
```

What happens is that the `ResourceLoader` takes the original path ("res://icon.png"), looks whether such a file was previously imported (looks into `.import` directory), and retrieves the resource for you, so it doesn't really load the original file anymore.

Now, the problem with such approach is that this is limited to the project's virtual resource filesystem ("res://"). If you need to load any external files outside of "res://" in exported projects, this will fail, because all of the game contents get packed into `game.pck`. Methods like `Image.load()` are not even aware of this virtual filesystem in Godot and rely on the typical OS-specific filesystem methods for loading data (using the internal `FileAccess` class, aka `File` in GDScript), and not GDScript's `load()`. The reason it works in the editor is because those image files are still there on your filesystem. In theory, you can also disable automatic re-import, delete those original files outside of the editor, and still able to run your game. 🙂

> Lastly what should someone do if they truly intend for an image/texture to be loaded from `user://`?

For best results, you have to replicate the same import process manually at run-time, because most of the import methods are only available in the editor. Yes, I know, this can be a big limitation in your project if your game takes advantage of user-generated content. And the most practical and feasible way to "import" textures at run-time is by loading an `Image` and creating an `ImageTexture` from that. 🙂 

The procedure would be the same as in the first snippet in this PR, but use "user://" instead. You have to clearly define what content would be able to be loaded externally and design your game architecture accordingly.

body:
The logic behind my proposed change is to make things consistent when the body hits the side of a platform. From the previous discussion, it was decided that it would always go through in this case. That could be ensured for more cases by adding a little flexibility for mathematical approximation in this check.

The case I'm talking about is not 90°, but 180° rotation (platform upside-down).

Looks mostly good! Most of my comments are just about cleaning up code. 

I noticed 3 issues while testing:

1. If the GPUParticles3D is set to use ``local_coords`` then all collisions will be offset by the local transform of the GPUParticles3D.

2. If the GPUParticlesCollisionHeightField is following the camera, it doesn't follow in the y direction. so if the HeightField is rotated it no longer follows the camera.

3. when GPUParticlesCollisionHeightField is following the camera it is wasting a lot of resources by rendering the heightfield behind the camera, instead it should follow the position and rotation of the camera so that it is only covering a small area that is outside the camera's field of view.

> The fact that nanosleep() sleeps for a relative interval can be
       problematic if the call is repeatedly restarted after being
       interrupted by signals, since the time between the interruptions
       and restarts of the call will lead to drift in the time when the

So I'm wondering if we should instead switch to `clock_nanosleep` as suggested.

body:
Godot projects didn't support .NET Standard at first. Today we still default to `net472` in 3.2 to avoid breaking projects, but 3.2 supports it and 4.0 defaults to `netstandard2.1`.
Regarding `GodotTools`, .NET Standard is definitely preferred, but some projects have .NET Framework dependencies like `Microsoft.Build` hence why they target .NET Framework instead (.NET Standard projects can't have .NET Framework dependencies).
The reason we target `netstandard2.0` rather than `netstandard2.1` is because the latter is only fully supported in `net480` (.NET Framework 4.8) which our projects don't target as it was too bleeding edge back then.
Also .NET Standard 2.0 is recommended over 2.1 for the best compatibility (as said before `net472` can't reference `netstandard2.1`) so `GodotTools.IdeMessaging` likely won't change as it's used outside of Godot too (VS extension).

body:
I like `randv_ring`, and perhaps `range` is not the best choice here because it might falsely suggest that it's going to generate *arc*/*sector* range rather than *radius* range. That said, going for consistency with existing `*_range` methods could actually hurt the meaning.

Except that if we rename `randv_range_circle` to `randv_ring`, if you have `min_radius == max_radius`, then it's not really a ring anymore, but restricted to circle's boundary, there's a reason why godotengine/godot-proposals#1731 lists `rand_point_on_circle` to handle this case, both in terms of use cases and effeciency.

That way, `randv_circle_range` and `randv_ring_range` could be added later to restrict the generation to a *sector*, but that's likely overkill for Godot, and I'm not sure how trivial it is to implement it. But then again, `randv_circle_sector` and `randv_ring_sector` would probably make more sense anyways (mostly talking about extending `RandomNumberGenerator` via modules now).

That said, there are many different ways to name this, I'm fine with either (but prefer less verbose names myself).

I did some brief research, and found this: https://android.jlelse.eu/android-api-level-backward-and-forward-compatibility-10e6d31cb848

At least as I understand it, the `compileSdkVersion` determines which methods/types are available during compilation, but the `minSdkVersion` determines the minimum required API level required for the app to run on a device. As long as you perform adequate runtime checks before calling API methods which may not be available on the device, then everything should be cool.

I just tested this change on my old Nexus 5 (running Marshmallow / API 23) and `OS.get_window_safe_area()` works as expected (returning the full screen rectangle). :man_shrugging:

body:
Negative values for colors don't actually exist because negative light doesn't exist. However, there are use cases where it makes sense in code, for example adding a color of `(-0.1, 0.2, 0.3)` would change the color by removing 10% red, adding 20% green, and adding 30% blue.

Not sure what's the desired behavior, but I guess there isn't much harm in supporting this. Currently the C# code does support this, since `r8` etc are signed ints with no clamping, so it's currently inconsistent with the C++ code.
author: aaronfranke

body:
It's a bit abusing the `Color` data type to represent a `ΔColor` (i.e. `Color2 - Color1`) though, which has different mathematical properties (and physical properties, since a `Δx` is not a physical value), just like `K` (Kelvin) and `ΔK` have different properties.

I don't think that making the `Color` boundaries flexible to support deltas is a good idea, as it means you can actually end up with negative Colors in rendering code, which breaks a lot of assumptions.

If you want to do the above, the right way would be `- (0.1, 0, 0) + (0, 0.2, 0.3)`. Might be less elegant but it doesn't open up a can worms :)

If we had `Vector4` support in GDScript, we could instead allow using it for `ΔColor`, so you could do `Color + Vector4` to apply a delta. But I'm not sure that use case is significant enough to warrant doing this.

body:
`MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED` is a union (`3`) of the captured state (`2`) and the hidden state (`1`). `MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED_VISIBLE` (`2`) is just the captured state without the hidden state (so it's visible). Captured should usually imply hidden, which is why I made the exposed `MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED` have the hidden state.

So `& MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED_VISIBLE` (aka `& 2`) will handle both `2` and `3`.

author: aaronfranke

body:
I'm not sure I get why this has to be so complicated. Wouldn't it be easier to just have e.g.
```
MOUSE_MODE_HIDDEN = 1,
MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED = 2,
MOUSE_MODE_CONFINED = 4,
```
Then check these bits as needed in the code.

I think the MOUSE_MODE_GRABBED and MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED (your version) just makes things more confusing, not less.

There is no need for MOUSE_MODE_VISIBLE, as by definition if HIDDEN is not set it is visible, and checking bitwise flags for absolute values is bad practice (what happens if you add a new flag?).

And having MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED_VISIBLE as 2 seems ridiculous because you can then have non-sensical flag combinations, of a HIDDEN and VISIBLE mouse mode...

If on the other hand the idea is to enforce state, you could use e.g. an encapsulated class / struct, either using the above flags or something like:
```
class MouseMode
{
bool visible; // or hidden
enum CaptureState
{
CS_NORMAL,
CS_CAPTURED,
CS_CONFINED,
};
public:
// accessors
// ...
}
```
and use the accessor functions to enforce state.

Another option is combining an enum and flags in the same bits (e.g. use bits 0-3 for an enum, and 4-7 for flags etc). But this is usually to save memory / pass something smaller around, and not really something user-friendly unless you have accessor functions.

That said I'm not really familiar with how MouseMode is used throughout Godot, there may be other considerations.

body: So thinking about it more, something bigger than 8-bits is needed (could also be 16-bit, doesn't really matter), since the algorithm requires you to shift beyond the 8-bits of a byte. `v` is always going to end up being 0 or 255. In the case that `v = 0` at the end of the loop (i.e. the byte arrays are the same), then `v ^ 0 = 0`. If the result is a byte, then when you subtract 1 from it, you get `b11111111`. If it's a uint32, it's `b11111111111111111111111111111111`. So when we shift past the bounds of a byte, it's either going to be 1 or 0. It's a good obfuscation for sure, but looking deeper at different implementations, it seems that the Go implementation is currently the only major language that implements it this way. All the other major languages that I looked at seem to just `return v== 0`. For now, I'll simplify it as such until I have more time to more deeply look into this.

Well now it's incorrect IMO, and indeed just duplicates the value of the enum itself. It doesn't match what you have in InputMapEditor.

My understanding is that there's two representation:

- On a SDL gamepad, you have two sticks (left and right). The left stick has X axis (index 0) and Y axis (index 1). The right stick has X axis (index 2) and Y axis (index 3).
- On a generic joystick, **if the input map editor is correct**, you can have any number of **sticks** (well up to 4 for us), each with X and Y axes. So there index 0 is the X axis of the stick no. 0, 1 is the Y axis of the stick no. 0, 2 is the X axis of the stick no. 1, 3 is the Y axis of the stick no. 1, 4 is the X axis of the stick no. 2, etc.

So when I wrote "index", I referred to the **stick** index, not the **axis** index which would be the same as the enum values (2 times more axes than sticks).
author: akien-mga

body:
Each joystick has two axes, and each axis has two directions. What's confusing is that there is a left and a right joystick, which each have a left and a right direction.

The SDL game controller mappings support 6 axes: 2 joysticks (left and right) with 2 axes each (X and Y) with 2 directions each (+ve and -ve) and two triggers, each with its own axis and only positive values. These six axes are what the `enum` corresponds to.

On the other hand, Godot provides support for 5 joysticks, 10 axes and 20 directions. The map editor provides those 20 directions as options: and prepends each of them with the axis number and a `+` or `-` for the direction:

![Screenshot_2020-11-19_14-24-05](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9253928/99678818-237e0880-2a73-11eb-83ec-334b4c45e6ed.png)

The way I see it, we have two options:
1. Drop the "Corresponds to axis x":
- JOY_AXIS_LEFT_X: Game controller left joystick x-axis.
- JOY_AXIS_LEFT_Y:  Game controller left joystick y-axis.
- JOY_AXIS_RIGHT_X: Game controller right joystick x-axis.
- JOY_AXIS_RIGHT_Y: Game controller right joystick y-axis.
- JOY_AXIS_TRIGGER_LEFT: Game controller left trigger axis.
- JOY_AXIS_TRIGGER_RIGHT: Game controller right trigger axis.
2. Change them to:
- JOY_AXIS_LEFT_X: Game controller left joystick x-axis. Corresponds to Joystick 0 x-axis.
- JOY_AXIS_LEFT_Y:  Game controller left joystick y-axis. Corresponds to Joystick 0 y-axis.
- JOY_AXIS_RIGHT_X: Game controller right joystick x-axis. Corresponds to Joystick 1 x-axis.
- JOY_AXIS_RIGHT_Y: Game controller right joystick y-axis. Corresponds to Joystick 1 y-axis.
- JOY_AXIS_TRIGGER_LEFT: Game controller left trigger axis. Corresponds to Joystick 2 right.
- JOY_AXIS_TRIGGER_RIGHT: Game controller right trigger axis. Corresponds to Joystick 2 down.

I prefer the first option, drop the "Corresponds to axis x" i.e. the way it is currently (without this PR). The second option, although correct, adds confusion, because the triggers are positive only.

body:
`int` is probably fine here as the max size is 1024 * sizeof (int), but in general when using the stack, akien is absolutely right, because the stack can be of very limited size, platform dependent, and how much room you have 'depends'. It absolutely is not the same as general memory.

See e.g. here, suggesting historical figures of 8K being possible on old mobile:
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/1859327/android-stack-size

So 1024 * 8 byte int = 8K, blown stack. Whereas 1024 * 2 byte uint16_t = slightly safer, but still likely to blow such a small stack.

More realistically, modern times I would expect around a 1 meg+, especially on desktop:
https://pspdfkit.com/blog/2019/android-large-memory-requirements/

But this is not just for your function.

In short, alloca is great but make sure you know what you are doing, and beware of anything that might be called recursively. This kind of thing is why the compiler refuses to compile with a FORCE_INLINE.

body:
I'm not 100% sure of what's going on with BPTC and it looks like the behavior is different in master vs. 3.2 too.

I think `texture_format/bptc` and `texture_format/no_bptc_fallbacks` are obsolete because the fallback system was removed, BPTC was rolled into the S3TC feature, and the choice of whether to enable BPTC became a project option, but that also means that "S3TC" in the export options is a misnomer because it controls both formats.

AFAIK as of 0565adb20ff01a758c5ae8e4534a2cb7f07952df (and then fixed by pull 21256), BPTC was compacted into the S3TC option and changed to use the `rendering/vram_compression/import_bptc` project setting to control whether it's enabled at all.

When the project option is enabled, then `compress/bptc_ldr` on the texture import settings also affects whether or not it's used for RGB textures, but the default AND available options for that setting appear to be different in master and 3.2.  I'll need to have some discussion about that, because I think Disabled is a bad default, but what the sensible is may depend on the project...

body:
There is a native C# way to do this: `System.Net.WebUtility.UrlEncode` (and the inverse `System.Net.WebUtility.UrlDecode`). EDIT: Actually `System.Uri.EscapeDataString` and `System.Uri.UnescapeDataString` are better.

However, in `System.Net.WebUtility.UrlEncode` spaces are encoded as `+`, while in `System.Uri.EscapeDataString` and in Godot, spaces are encoded as `%20`. This seems to be a [hot debate](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/1634271/url-encoding-the-space-character-or-20). There is no option in `System.Net.WebUtility.UrlEncode` to make it use `%20` (I opened a feature request here: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/45328), and `%20` seems to be broadly accepted as the better format. Both are valid URLs, and the GDScript-encoded version being decoded in C# is fine, but the `System.Net.WebUtility.UrlEncode`-encoded version being decoded in GDScript is not valid because GDScript does not currently handle this alternate format. C# is able to decode both formats, but GDScript can't decode the `+` format.

One idea is to wrap around `System.Uri.EscapeDataString` and `System.Uri.UnescapeDataString` and encourage their usage, which would give the same behavior as GDScript. The `%20` format can be decoded everywhere.

Another idea is that we can tweak the decoding in GDScript to handle the `+` scheme. If that is done, both GDScript and C# will be able to decode from each other and themselves, even though they will encode different things. This does change the behavior if something expected `+` to be `+` and not `%2B`, but I don't think anyone uses this format.

We can actually do both of these things at the same time. If we do only the first one, then C# `string.HTTPEscape` will encode the same as GDScript, but then GDScript still won't handle the alternate format such as if `System.Net.WebUtility.UrlEncode` is used directly. If we only do the second option, then the decode methods would be intercompatible, but the encode methods would give different results. If we do both, then I think that solves all of the problems. EDIT: #43978

`set_stream_peer` was used in `3.2` by the script editor debugger, but that's no longer the case in `4.0`.
The thing that worries me about this change, is that having the error check there, would make it impossible to clear the `PacketPeerStream` so it can be reused from GDScript:
```gdscript
ppeer.set_stream_peer(_stream)
# [Do things]
# Disconnect
ppeer.set_stream_peer(null)
_stream.disconnect_from_host()
```
Of course one can create a new `ppeer`, but I still think it's weird, and I would rather remove the `_set_stream_peer` version.

body:
To be clear, I'm asking about the benefit of smaller in memory sizes for meshes. I don't think it's possible to use a smaller type for vertices. [Since you decided to only have have one (compressed) mesh format.]

> As an example, a static PBR-ready mesh typically requires POSITION (12 bytes), TEXCOORD (8 bytes), NORMAL (12 bytes) and TANGENT (16 bytes) for each vertex, for a total of 48 bytes. With this extension, it is possible to use SHORT to store position and texture coordinate data (8 and 4 bytes, respectively) and BYTE to store normal and tangent data (4 bytes each), for a total of 20 bytes per vertex with often negligible quality impact.
author: fire

body:
Godot 4.0 uses:
* 12 bytes for position. At some point we added quantizing for this as optional, but it just generally looks bad and users had a lot of problems. Meshes had visible seams, small details get deformed easily, etc. Its just not worh it.
* 4 bytes for normal (Godot 4.0 uses ARGB2101010)
* 4 bytes for tangent (also ARGB2101010)
* 8 bytes for UV. Again, we s upported having less, but to be honest users nowadays mostly use larger textures than 1024, so using half float for UV looks pretty terrible.

This way, Godot uses 12+4+4+8=28 bytes per vertex instead of 20. Its honestly not much of a problem and things just work.
